name: PT Bukalapak.com Tbk.

frontmatter.title: Bukalapak: the cash is worth more than the price
frontmatter.summary: Bukalapak has become an Emtek-controlled, gaming-led digital distribution business trading far below its net cash. The operating stub is near breakeven on adjusted EBITDA and generates positive operating cash flow, while the balance sheet holds liquidity larger than the market capitalisation. We initiate at BUY: the target implies a large re-rating, but the catalyst is capital return or group action, not organic growth; without it the discount can persist.
thesis: The market capitalisation is below the reported net cash position, so investors are being paid to own an operating business that is close to breakeven [S0].
Gaming is now the business: it is the large majority of revenue, grew strongly in the latest nine months and turned adjusted EBITDA positive in Q1-2026 [S9, S6].

The discount reflects governance, not solvency: Emtek controls the company through a 11.1% direct stake inside a 63.2% insider bloc, consolidates it, pays no dividend and has historically retained the cash [S10, S5, S13].

A larger buyback, a special distribution or a group-level transaction is the re-rating catalyst; the October 2025 programme was capped at a small fraction of the liquidity and had to be completed by January 2026 [S14].

The balance-sheet impairment is priced once, at the bear probability, in a bridge that every scenario shares; no case credits the liquid assets at face, and moving the full charge into the bear alone leaves the weighted target unchanged [S0, S11].

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results and any update on capital allocation
Any new buyback or capital-return announcement after the October 2025 programme expired
AGMS dividend decision and board composition
Further Emtek group stake disclosures above the reporting threshold

blocks.text: We initiate coverage of PT Bukalapak.com Tbk with a **BUY** rating and a twelve-month target price of Rp190, implying 84.5% upside from the Rp103 close on 10 November 2026 [S0]. The target is the probability-weighted output of an FCFF DCF (weighted 80%) and an EV/sales cross-check (weighted 20%); the base-case intrinsic value is Rp189 per share [S0].

The variant view is simple and uncomfortable: BUKA trades below its own liquidity. At Rp103 the market capitalisation is IDR9,458.9bn, while the latest balance sheet carries cash and investments larger than that market value [S0, S2]. The operating business explains very little of the gap: FY2025A revenue was IDR6,510bn but EBITDA was only IDR-66bn, and our FY2026E EBITDA is IDR45bn [S0]. The DCF therefore values the operating enterprise at a small fraction of the equity, and the balance sheet does the rest [S0].

What moves the value is not revenue growth. It is whether the cash is returned or redeployed. The three drivers we underwrite are: first, the durability of gaming distribution revenue, which reached 4,881 IDR bn in the first nine months of 2026 [S9]; second, the cost base, where adjusted EBITDA turned positive at 4.0 IDR bn in Q1-2026 [S6]; and third, capital allocation, where Emtek's direct stake is 11.1% inside a 63.2% insider bloc and no dividend has ever been paid [S10, S0]. A fourth, unquantifiable driver is an Emtek group transaction that crystallises the balance sheet [S5].

The target does not assume the cash is returned in full. The gross equity bridge carries the liquid assets at face value and then deducts one probability-weighted charge, equal to the gap between those liquid assets and the market capitalisation, at the bear-case probability: the market's own measure of what a governance or capital-destruction event costs, not a number we invented [S0, S11]. The base case remains that the cash is reachable; the bear case is that it is not, and that case is in the arithmetic, weighted at the bear probability in the shared bridge, rather than only in the prose.

Indonesian listed technology names that raised large IPO proceeds and then shrank their operating footprint often trade at persistent discounts to book and cash. The discount is a governance phenomenon rather than a solvency one, and it closes when control changes hands or when a capital-return policy is credibly established. This pattern is background and is not part of the quantified case.

Bukalapak began life as one of Indonesia's largest e-commerce marketplaces, but the business that remains is a digital distribution platform. The company now operates through gaming, online-to-offline, retail, investment and corporate segments; gaming is the growth engine and the others are in run-off [S9]. In October 2025 the group consolidated its gaming lines under a holding entity, Multi Realm Games, which now houses the gaming business [S7]. That structure signals that management sees gaming as the core rather than a side bet.

The revenue mix has inverted. In the first nine months of 2026, gaming generated 4,881 IDR bn of the 5,640 IDR bn total, while online-to-offline produced 484 IDR bn and retail 209 IDR bn [S9]. Gaming was the large majority of the 3,990 IDR bn first-half revenue, with the segment at 3,480 IDR bn [S11]. The first quarter alone showed gaming at 2,100 IDR bn of 2,370 IDR bn of revenue [S6]. In other words, BUKA is no longer an e-commerce company with a gaming add-on; it is a gaming top-up and distribution business with a residual marketplace.

The operating model is low-margin and working-capital-light. Gaming distribution buys digital goods and resells them, which produces high revenue and thin gross margins; the group gross margin is only 8.1% in our forecast [S0]. Because the product is digital and settlement is fast, the business needs little fixed capital: capex was a fraction of one percent of revenue in FY2025A [S0]. The cost base is people and marketing, and management has been cutting both. The workforce fell by several hundred in FY2025 and the physical marketplace footprint was closed [S4].

The competitive position is that of a scaled challenger in a fragmented distribution market. BUKA is not the largest e-commerce platform in Indonesia, and it does not claim to be; it is one of a handful of scaled digital-goods distributors with direct relationships with game publishers and payment channels [S7]. The moat, such as it is, comes from distribution density and publisher relationships rather than from consumer brand or switching costs. That is a thin moat, and we do not underwrite a widening one [S9].

Ownership and group structure are central to the story. Emtek Group, through PT Elang Mahkota Teknologi Tbk, is the controlling shareholder; its direct stake rose to 11.1% after an October 2026 open-market purchase of 424 m shares, inside an insider bloc of 63.2% [S10, S0]. The operative fact is not the size of the direct stake but consolidation: Emtek has consolidated BUKA into its own financial statements since February 2025, and BUKA's total assets represented a large share of Emtek's consolidated assets [S5]. Consolidation under the accounting standard requires control, so the group directs the board and capital allocation whatever the percentage held. That makes BUKA a subsidiary of a listed media-and-technology group, not an independent company, and it explains why the market prices the cash at a discount [S10, S5].

The relevant industry is Indonesian digital commerce and digital-goods distribution. The marketplace segment is mature and consolidated around a few scaled platforms, while gaming top-ups and digital vouchers remain fragmented among distributors, payment aggregators and telco-linked channels [S7]. BUKA competes in the distribution layer, where scale in publisher relationships and payment rails matters more than consumer traffic [S9]. The addressable pool grows with smartphone penetration, digital payments and gaming spend, but the distributor's share of that pool is a thin spread over the underlying goods.

The macro backdrop is mixed for a domestic consumer platform. The rupiah is forecast at Rp18,350/USD against the dollar, which matters because the company holds most of its liquidity in foreign currency [S2]. Bank Indonesia's policy rate is forecast at 5.75% and CPI at 3.28%, so real consumer incomes are not collapsing but are not buoyant either [S0]. Real GDP growth of 5.29% supports digital spend in aggregate, while a weaker rupiah raises the local-currency value of the FX cash: the group booked a net foreign-exchange gain of IDR872bn in the first nine months of 2026, mostly unrealised [S13]. We neither credit the deck's weaker-rupiah path in the base nor deduct a stronger-rupiah loss, so the currency treatment is neutral in both directions; the risk section says what that means for the scenarios.

Competition is intense at the distribution layer. Mobile top-up aggregators, e-wallet-linked voucher sellers and telco channels all compete for the same publisher inventory, and gross margins are structurally thin [S9]. The five-forces picture is unfavourable on rivalry and supplier power: game publishers have several distribution channels and can set commercial terms, while buyers are price-sensitive and have low switching costs. Barriers to entry are moderate because publisher agreements and payment integration take time, but they are not proprietary. That is why we model a flat gross margin rather than an expanding one [S9].

Regulation is a secondary influence rather than the main driver. The company operates under Indonesian company and capital-market rules, reports as a listed issuer and is subject to exchange disclosure requirements; the exchange has queried the composition of its foreign-currency cash, which shows that disclosure scrutiny is active [S2]. There is no concession, licence or tariff that sets the economics of the business, unlike a commodity producer. The regulatory risk is therefore about disclosure, related-party dealing and minority protection rather than about pricing.

The moat assessment is deliberately modest. BUKA has distribution reach and publisher relationships, but it does not have a network effect that strengthens with each user, nor switching costs that lock in merchants. Its scale is real but contestable [S9]. The industry card's test is whether excess returns are protected by a named mechanism; here the honest answer is that the operating business earns close to its cost of capital at best, and the investment case rests on the balance sheet rather than on franchise value; the operating business is a distribution pipe rather than a toll road, so we do not attribute a durable moat to it [S0].

The historical record is volatile because of one-off items. Revenue rose from IDR3,618bn in FY2022A to IDR6,510bn in FY2025A, with the jump concentrated in FY2025A as gaming scaled [S0]. Gross profit did not follow: FY2025A gross profit was IDR519bn, a low gross margin, because the growth came from low-margin distribution [S0]. Reported net profit was IDR3,142bn in FY2025A, but that figure was driven by investment gains and the disposal of financial assets rather than by operations; the company itself described it as its first profit after years of losses, helped by investment value [S8].

Our forecast reproduces the last actual's economics rather than extrapolating the one-off. We model FY2026E revenue of IDR7,454bn, growth of 14.5%, anchored on the 5,640 IDR bn of nine-month revenue already reported [S9]. The quarterly path is not smooth and we do not smooth it: Q1 revenue was 2,370 IDR bn, the first half as a whole was 3,990 IDR bn and the nine months were 5,640 IDR bn, so Q2 and Q3 each ran at roughly two-thirds of Q1 [S6, S11, S9]. Gaming shows the same step-down, from 2,100 IDR bn in Q1 to 4,881 IDR bn over nine months [S6, S9]. The Q1 level was inflated by seasonal game launches; the Q2-Q3 run-rate is what we carry forward. Q4 was the strongest quarter of FY2025 and our FY2026E revenue implies a fourth quarter only slightly above the prior-year quarter, which is far below what the gaming segment delivered over the nine months, when it produced 4,881 IDR bn of 5,640 IDR bn of revenue: the base already assumes the gaming trend flattens, not that it compounds [S9, S0]. Gross margin stays at 8.1%, total opex at 8.6% of revenue, and D&A at 1.1% [S0]. That combination produces FY2026E EBITDA of IDR45bn and a small negative EBIT of IDR-37bn, which is consistent with the Q1-2026 adjusted EBITDA of 4.0 IDR bn [S6].

The path to profitability in our model is non-operating, and the reported number will not look like the model's. Interest income on the large cash balance covers the operating loss, which is why the model shows a small FY2026E net profit of IDR817bn [S0]. The reported nine-month result is a loss of 885 IDR bn, because it carries the investment fair-value losses that the model excludes through a zero other-non-operating line [S9, S3]. We therefore do not print a FY2026E P/E: the reported earnings line is dominated by a mark-to-market item we deliberately keep out of the operating value, and the model's profit and the reported loss cannot be reconciled without it. The DCF is EBIT-based, so no part of the valuation depends on that line. Read adjusted EBITDA, which was IDR11bn over the nine months [S9], and operating cash flow, not reported net income.

Cash generation is the reassuring part. LTM operating cash flow is positive at roughly the level of EBITDA plus a working-capital release, and capex is minimal, so the operating business is not consuming the cash pile [S0]. The company also bought back stock: the share count fell by about a tenth during FY2025, and a buyback programme of up to IDR421bn — the remainder of an allocation approved in July 2025 — was announced in October 2025 [S14]. That programme had to be completed by 29 January 2026 [S14], so its cash cost is inside the reported September cash balance rather than still to come; no later programme had been announced in the sources we hold by the balance-sheet date. Buying back equity at a deep discount to liquid assets is the highest-return use of the cash available to any management team: every share retired at today's price transfers the gap between the price and liquid assets per share to the holders who remain, so a programme an order of magnitude larger would be strongly accretive per share, and the arithmetic is the same whether the shares are cancelled or held as treasury. The controller's own open-market purchase of 424 m shares at about the market price is evidence that the insiders see the same gap [S10]. The programme was small relative to the liquidity and time-limited, which is why it has not closed the discount on its own; the constraint is scale and willingness, not the logic of the trade [S14].

The balance sheet is the crux. The latest reported balance sheet carries cash and investments well in excess of debt, and net cash is larger than the market capitalisation [S0]. The composition needs care because the aggregator and the filing use different labels, and we take the filing: the 30 September 2026 notes put cash and cash equivalents at IDR15,564bn, about five-eighths of total assets [S2]. The pack's cash line for the same date is higher, and it labels the difference as short-term placements and other current financial assets. We do not credit that difference anywhere in the valuation, because no archived source documents those balances line by line; it is disclosed here as an unsourced item rather than credited in the bridge. Crediting it would have raised the per-share value materially and unsourced, so the bridge uses the primary cash figure, adds the investment portfolio the engine carries separately, and then deducts the probability-weighted impairment described in the valuation section. Of the cash and equivalents, IDR12,900bn was held in foreign currency [S2]. Management's letter says that FX balance is held untuk kebutuhan operasional dan optimalisasi likuiditas, for operating needs and liquidity optimisation, and that it did not come from IPO proceeds: the net IPO proceeds of IDR21,330bn have been used per the AGMS-approved allocation, with IDR4,280bn left at end-2025 [S13, F20]. Read plainly, that is a management claim that the balance is deployable rather than restricted, not proof that it will be returned; the two are different propositions, and the gap between them is the investment case rather than a detail.

Earnings-quality screens raise two flags but not a kill. First, the accrual content of the profit is the whole profit: FY2025A net profit of IDR3,142bn sits against an EBITDA of IDR-66bn and a modelled free cash flow to the firm of IDR-506bn, the gap being non-operating income of IDR2,540bn and interest income of IDR818bn [S0]. The three-year accruals ratio the house card asks for cannot be computed from what is archived here: no consolidated cash-flow statement for FY2024 to FY2026 is in the source set, and the house rule forbids backing a fact with the aggregator alone, so there is no sourced operating-cash-flow denominator to print. We state that as a gap in the record rather than describing the ratio qualitatively, and we flag that the FY2025 profit is accrual-heavy by construction, which is the direction the card is designed to catch. On operating cash flow the business is cash-generative at a small scale, which is why we classify this as optics-class rather than a manipulation flag. Second, the investment portfolio has produced large fair-value losses, with the portfolio down sharply in the first half of 2026 [S11]. Related-party revenue and balances could not be quantified either: the consolidated LK is not archived in this workspace, so the related-party note could not be read, and we say so rather than asserting the exposure is immaterial [S5]. The board and notation status is taken from the market data pack only, not verified against an exchange announcement, and the auditor opinion is not qualified in the sources reviewed [S0].

The table prints two cash definitions, and the reconciliation belongs here rather than in a footnote. The projected net debt line of IDR-22,043bn at FY2026E is built on the data pack's cash line, which includes short-term placements and other current financial assets, and that is the balance the projected cash flow and the projected balance sheet use. The valuation bridge uses the filing's cash and cash equivalents of IDR15,564bn at 30 September 2026 [S2] against debt of IDR113bn, and the interest line of IDR954bn is earned on the inclusive balance rather than on the filing figure. The two numbers are not two cash piles: the IDR-22,043bn above is the projected line on the pack's definition, and the net cash that produces the target is the filing's, about IDR15,564bn less debt. The gap between them has two parts. The first is definitional: the pack's cash line includes short-term placements and other current financial assets that the notes classify outside cash and equivalents, and that part runs through the pack's annual series as well. The second is timing: the projection runs the fiscal year from the FY2025A cash line of IDR21,199bn rather than from the 30 September filing, and adds the modelled flow for the rest of FY2026 to reach IDR22,155bn, so part of the difference is modelled cash that has not been reported. Only the first part is a definitional difference. No part of the DCF, the bridge or the target uses the inclusive balance, and the interest income that the projected P&L shows is not capitalised anywhere in the valuation.

Capital allocation is the swing factor for the equity. The group has no dividend record, returns cash through time-limited buybacks, and holds the rest in financial investments [S0, S14]. The investment portfolio has lost value — IDR1,740bn in the first half of 2026 alone — which is a real cost to shareholders and the strongest argument that the cash is worth less than face value [S11]. Against that, the operating business is close to breakeven and the FX cash has been stable; the cash is not being burned by operations [S0]. We therefore carry the liquid assets at their gross face value in the equity bridge and deduct a single probability-weighted impairment, sized to the market-implied haircut and weighted at the bear probability, so destructive deployment is priced rather than only described, as the valuation section sets out.

The industry method set is a DCF (FCFF, terminal value) weighted 80% and EV/sales weighted 20%, with a peer-median multiple [S0]. That combination fits a business with a small, thin-margin operating stub and a large non-operating balance sheet: the DCF captures the operating economics and the cash bridge, while EV/sales anchors the operating value to what the market pays for comparable distribution platforms [S0]. A P/E or EV/EBITDA cross-check would be meaningless here because EBITDA is close to zero and reported earnings are distorted by investment items [S0].

The cost of capital is built from the house macro deck and a company beta, and the build should be shown in full because it does not read off the headline inputs. The risk-free rate is 7.4%, the mature-market ERP 4.2%, the Indonesia country premium 2.5% and the tax rate 22.0% [S0]. A 1.6% default-spread offset is then deducted from the premium for a balance sheet that is mostly net cash, which is the step that reconciles the inputs: 7.4% plus 0.95 times the sum of the ERP and the country premium, less that offset, gives a COE of 12.2% and a WACC of 12.2% [S0]. We use an unlevered beta of 0.95 rather than the higher industry default because the balance sheet is predominantly net cash and the operating business is a near-breakeven distributor; the WACC therefore sits below the covered peer set but inside the house rupiah band, which is the check that matters, and we argue the beta rather than the band. The per-share effect is small against the cash bridge, as the sensitivity table shows, but the reader should know it is a choice and not an output. The debt weight is negligible because debt is immaterial [S0].

The DCF produces an operating enterprise value of IDR520bn and a value of Rp161 per share [S0]. Terminal value is 50.5% of the enterprise value, which is high as a share but small in absolute terms: the explicit-period cash flows are thin because the margin is thin, so the whole operating number is small either way [S0]. The equity bridge adds the LK's cash and cash equivalents of IDR15,564bn and the investment portfolio, less debt and less the probability-weighted impairment, which is why the per-share value sits above the operating enterprise value. Book equity of IDR26,118bn exceeds the bridged total because the net operating assets are carried far above what a thin-margin distributor earns on them: they are not valued at zero, they are valued at the DCF's enterprise value, and we do not add book value on top of an enterprise value that already includes them. Part of the H1-2026 investing outflow went into the gaming build-out under Multi Realm Games and part into financial placements; the operating part is what the DCF prices, and the placements are in the cash line [S11, S7].

The investment portfolio in the bridge is not an unexplained aggregate. The one listed position the archive identifies is a 11.5% stake in PT Allo Bank Indonesia (BBHI), held since January 2022 when BBHI shares traded above Rp5,000 each and now quoted at Rp900, down nearly two-fifths since the start of 2026 and more than four-fifths below the entry price [S11]. The position is therefore marked well below cost, and the portfolio's first-half loss of IDR1,740bn is that write-down passing through the P&L [S11]. We credit the pack's carrying value of the whole portfolio and do not add the BBHI quotation on top of it: the stake is already carried inside total assets, so adding it again would double count. What the archive does not contain is the investment note, so we cannot list the remaining holdings or split the aggregate between the listed stake and the unlisted positions. That is the limit of the evidence and we state it rather than presenting the aggregate as verified composition.

The card's growth bridge is the right test for this name, and it fails as a compounder rather than as a forecast. Growth equals reinvestment rate times return on incremental invested capital. Reinvestment here is capex of IDR30bn less depreciation of IDR82bn plus a working-capital movement of IDR-87bn, which is negative: the operating business is not putting investor capital in, it is releasing it while its fixed base shrinks. NOPAT is negative because EBIT is IDR-37bn and the tax charge is levied on a profit before tax that interest income creates, so the product cannot be built as a positive number at all. What growth there is comes from publisher inventory and channel access that suppliers finance, not from capital we are being asked to fund, and it earns an incremental margin that is a rounding error on revenue. The honest statement is that this is not a franchise compounding capital; it is a distribution spread carried alongside a balance sheet, and the DCF values it accordingly.

Fade discipline has nothing to bite on. EBIT is negative in every explicit year, including IDR-26bn in the last one, so the business never earns an excess return on capital inside the forecast and there is no positive excess return to fade. We do not name a fade year for that reason, and we do not claim a moat mechanism that would justify delaying one: the distribution density argument in the industry section is contestable and we do not underwrite it widening. The terminal value therefore capitalises a distribution spread at roughly zero economic profit, and the risk in it runs the other way — if the spread compresses, the terminal value is too high, which the sensitivity table shows is immaterial against the balance sheet.

The multiple-survival test says the target does not lean on multiple expansion. The terminal value capitalises FY2035E EBITDA of IDR115bn; against our own enterprise value of IDR520bn the implied exit EV/EBITDA is roughly six to seven times and the entry multiple on the same basis is higher, so a rational buyer is not being asked to pay more at exit than at entry. On EBIT the test is meaningless in both directions because both the entry and exit EBIT are negative. At the market price the entry multiple is itself negative, because the market capitalisation is below net cash: a buyer there pays nothing for the operating business and receives the liquid assets at a discount. There is no growth premium anywhere in this valuation to survive or fail the test.

The EV/sales method, using a peer median multiple of 0.55 on LTM revenue, produces Rp199 per share, 24.1% above the DCF on a per-share basis [S0]. That per-share closeness is an artefact of the cash bridge, not agreement: the EV/sales method implies an operating enterprise value several times the DCF's, and it reaches a similar per-share number only because both methods then subtract the same net cash and the same impairment. On the operating business they disagree by a multiple, which is why the cross-check carries a reduced weight.

The EV/sales divergence is worth explaining rather than dismissing, and it is a divergence. The peer median is drawn from the covered Indonesian internet-platform names — the parent Emtek, GoTo, Blibli, Wifi and the voucher distributors M Cash and NFCX — several of which hold net cash, so the EV/sales multiple is low at 0.55 [S0]. The set is also not margin-matched: those platforms earn gross margins several times BUKA's 8.1%, so applying their revenue multiple to a distribution spread overstates the operating business by construction [S0, S9]. We keep the cross-check because it is the only method here that does not require a long explicit forecast for a stub, but we cut its weight from four tenths to one fifth and we do not present it as confirmation. The honest summary is that the operating business is worth somewhere between the two, and that neither number matters much against the cash.

What does today's price imply? At Rp103 the market capitalises BUKA at IDR9,458.9bn, well below the liquid assets on the last reported balance sheet [S0]. That gap is the size of the impairment we carry: the market-implied haircut is a sourced, observable quantity, and we apply it once, probability-weighted at the bear weight, in the bridge that every valuation method and every scenario shares. The charge is defined as liquid assets less market capitalisation, so it is a statement about the size of the market's discount rather than an independent estimate of a loss, and it re-strikes with the share price: a lower price widens the discount and raises the charge, a higher price shrinks it, and a re-rating toward our target would shrink it toward nothing. That is why the target is not independent of the price at which it is struck, and why it should be read as a convergence value rather than a fixed intrinsic worth. The base case does not credit the liquid assets at face: it carries the same probability-weighted charge as the bear and the bull, which is the arithmetic equivalent of charging the full amount in the bear alone and is why the weighted target is identical under the two constructions. What the base case does say is that we hold no filing that restricts the cash, only a management letter that says it is deployable [S13]; the bear says the market is right that a substantial part of it never reaches minorities, and that case moves the target. The result is a target of Rp190 against a price of Rp103, and a rating that is a statement about the most likely path rather than a guarantee about a binary governance outcome.

The valuation is therefore a bet on capital allocation, not on growth. If the group returns cash, the equity re-rates toward our target; if it retains and invests the cash at negative returns, the discount is deserved [S10, S11]. We do apply a governance and capital-impairment charge, but it is sourced and probability-weighted rather than an arbitrary haircut: its size is the gap the market already applies to the liquid assets and its weight is the bear probability, so it is a statement about the probability of the bad outcome, not a second discount on top of the market's. A reader who thinks that outcome is near-certain should not use our target at all, because the target gives it the bear weight and no more, and the valuation table shows the size of the charge that would then have to be applied in full. The one thing we will not do is average the condition away silently, which is why the charge sits in the bridge where it can be checked line by line.

The largest risk is governance and control, with high likelihood and high impact. Emtek controls the company through a 11.1% direct stake inside a 63.2% insider bloc and has consolidated BUKA since February 2025, which is the legal expression of that control [S10, S0, S5]. A controlling shareholder can direct related-party transactions, investment decisions and capital allocation, and minority holders have limited ability to force a distribution [S10]. The exchange has already queried the source and currency composition of the cash, which shows that the market and the regulator are watching this channel [S2]. This risk is the main reason the shares trade below cash, and it is not fully diversifiable. It is also priced: the valuation bridge deducts the market-implied impairment on liquid assets at the bear probability, so the risk sits inside the target rather than only inside this section.

The second risk is capital destruction in the investment portfolio. The portfolio lost IDR1,740bn in the first half of 2026 alone, and the reported nine-month loss of 885 IDR bn was driven by investment results rather than operations [S11, S9]. If the group continues to invest the balance sheet at negative real returns, the cash is worth less than face value and our target is too high. This is the strongest bear argument and it is the channel the valuation charge is built on: the impairment in the bridge is sized to the market-implied haircut and carried at the bear probability, so a reader can see the size of one bad outcome before it is weighted. The mitigant is that the portfolio is already marked down and the FX cash, which is the majority, has held value [S13].

The third risk is operating decay in gaming, and it is also a concentration risk. Gaming grew strongly in the latest nine months, but the distribution layer is competitive and margins are thin [S9], and the revenue is concentrated in a handful of publisher titles and in the app-store and payment channels that distribute them: a renegotiated publisher split or a channel fee change hits gross margin rather than revenue, which is why we treat it as a bear driver [S7, S9]. A slowdown in gaming spend, a change in publisher terms or a price war among top-up aggregators would hit revenue and could push EBITDA back below zero [S6]. We rate this medium-likelihood and medium-impact because the cost base has already been cut and the business is close to breakeven. The fourth risk is currency, and it cuts both ways: most of the cash is in foreign currency, so a sharply stronger rupiah reduces its rupiah value while a weaker rupiah raises it [S2]. The deck forecasts a weaker rupiah, which would be a tailwind; the group booked a net FX gain of IDR872bn in the first nine months of 2026 [S13, S0]. We credit neither direction in the base, so the treatment is neutral rather than one-sided.

Liquidity and funding risk are low. The company has no material debt, positive operating cash flow and a large liquidity buffer, so a funding crisis is not a plausible near-term scenario [S0]. The liquidity risk is about the shares, not the company: the free float is 28.7% and insider ownership is 63.2%, so the traded float is thin relative to the market capitalisation [S0]. That can amplify moves in both directions.

The scenarios stress the operating drivers by mirrored amounts: revenue growth plus or minus four percentage points and gross margin plus or minus one percentage point, with the base case carrying 45.0% of the weight and the bear 30.0% [S0]. The balance-sheet charge is not one of those shocks. The engine perturbs operating drivers only, so the charge sits in the valuation bridge, shared by all three cases, at the bear probability. The table therefore shows the engine's construction rather than a distribution of the balance-sheet outcome: every row is struck after the same probability-weighted charge, the bear row is the base plus the operating shock, and the spread between the rows is narrow because the operating enterprise is small next to the balance sheet, so no operating assumption can move the value much. To read the impairment as realised rather than as weighted, the reader has to use the construction rather than the rows: moving the full charge out of the shared bridge and into the bear alone, at the same probabilities, raises the base and the bull to face value, lowers the bear by the unweighted remainder of the charge, and leaves the weighted target exactly where it is. We print the equivalence instead of a fourth row because a scenario-specific bridge would require the engine to re-run the balance sheet inside each case, and it does not do that. The engine's own rows, on today's intrinsic value before the twelve-month cost-of-equity roll-forward, are bear Rp161, base Rp168 and bull Rp181; the forward values at a cost of equity of 12.2% are Rp180, Rp189 and Rp203, and the probability-weighted Rp190 is the target. So the bear above is the operating case on top of the shared charge, not on top of a second, full charge, and the bull is the operating case plus a capital-return decision carrying no cash premium above face, because we will not credit liquid assets above face without a source. That asymmetry is deliberate and it runs against us, not for us: the upside case is capped by face value while the downside case is not. It also sets the limit of the debate: even if the whole market-implied impairment were certain rather than probable, the value would still sit above today's share price, because the market's implied haircut is a discount to the liquid assets rather than a write-off of them. What remains above the price is the operating business plus the part of the balance sheet the market does not discount at all, and disputing that is disputing the size of the haircut, not its existence.

The signposts that would change our view are concrete. A larger buyback, a special dividend, a tender offer or a group restructuring that returns cash would be positive [S10]. A related-party acquisition, a large investment in an unrelated business or a further fall in the investment portfolio would be negative [S11]. A change in the controlling stake, up or down, would also matter because it changes the probability of a capital-return event [S10]. We monitor the quarterly cash balance, the FX share of cash and any new capital-return announcement against those signposts [S14].

Ownership is concentrated through control rather than through a single large direct stake. Emtek holds 11.1% directly after its October 2026 purchase of 424 m shares, inside an insider bloc of 63.2% with a free float of 28.7% [S10, S0]. Control rests on consolidation: Emtek has consolidated BUKA since February 2025, and the group directs strategy accordingly [S5]. The company is therefore a controlled subsidiary in practice, the interests of the controller and the minority are not automatically aligned, and group-level capital allocation can override BUKA-level priorities [S5].

Related-party gravity is the key governance issue. The parent is a listed media-and-technology group with its own capital needs, and BUKA's cash is the most liquid asset in the relationship [S5, S10]. Related-party revenue and balances could not be quantified: the consolidated LK for the September 2026 period is not archived in this workspace, so the related-party note was not available to read. We state that explicitly rather than claiming the exposure is small, and it is an open item for the next LK [S5]. The structural potential is there and the market prices it [S10]. The exchange's query on the foreign-currency cash is a reminder that disclosure of related-party and treasury matters is closely watched [S2]. There are no pledged controlling shares disclosed in the sources we reviewed [S0].

The dividend record is empty. BUKA has never paid a dividend, and the return mechanism has been buyback: a programme of up to IDR421bn announced in October 2025 and required to be completed by 29 January 2026 [S14]. That is a small fraction of the liquidity, it was time-limited, and it does not constitute a standing capital-return policy [S0, S14]. The auditor and opinion are not flagged as qualified in the data reviewed, and there is no special-monitoring board or notation letter in the market data [S0]. We treat the absence of a dividend as a governance signal rather than as a temporary choice, because the company has had cash for several years and has chosen to retain it [S13].

Board and control dynamics follow from consolidation. The controlling shareholder determines board composition and strategy, and minority holders have limited recourse beyond the annual meeting [S10, S5]. The buyback shows that management is attentive to per-share value, but its scale was modest and time-limited [S14]. We would view a credible capital-return framework, with a stated payout or a larger buyback, as the single most important governance improvement available to the company [S0].

ESG exposures are modest for a digital distributor. The direct environmental footprint is small because the business is asset-light and digital [S0]. The social and governance dimensions matter more: labour practices in a business that has cut staff, data privacy in a platform that handles payments, and minority protection under a controlling shareholder [S4, S10]. We do not assign a separate ESG valuation adjustment; the governance issues are already embedded in the discount and in our risk section [S0].

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 audited results, any new capital-return announcement after the October 2025 buyback expired, the annual meeting's dividend decision and further Emtek group stake disclosures [S0, S10, S14]. The FY2026 results will show whether gaming revenue held through the fourth quarter and whether the cost base stayed low [S9]. A new and larger buyback is the most direct route to closing the discount, so the next capital-allocation announcement is a live signal [S14]. A group-level transaction is not dated but is the highest-impact catalyst [S5].

The KPIs we monitor between updates are: gaming revenue and its share of the total, group gross margin, adjusted EBITDA, operating cash flow, the cash balance and the foreign-currency share of cash, the investment-portfolio fair value, any new capital-return announcement, and the controlling stake [S9, S2, S14]. We also monitor the rupiah, because a large part of the balance sheet is in foreign currency and the translation effect is material to reported equity [S13]. A deterioration in any of the first four would challenge the operating stub; a deterioration in the cash or governance metrics would challenge the thesis itself [S0].

The monitoring framework is deliberately simple. The operating business is small enough that a handful of KPIs capture it; the balance sheet is large enough that governance and capital allocation dominate the outcome [S0]. We will update the model when the FY2026 results are published and when there is a capital-allocation announcement, and we will revisit the rating if the cash is deployed in a way that impairs its value [S10]. Until then, the position is a valuation call on a controlled cash box with a thin operating business attached [S0].

bear.narrative: Operating decay plus a balance sheet the minorities do not control. Gaming growth stalls as mobile top-up aggregators and publisher terms tighten, so revenue growth is 4pp lower and gross margin 1pp lower than the base. The balance-sheet loss is not held at face value anywhere in the set: it is carried in the valuation bridge as one probability-weighted charge at the bear probability, which is the same arithmetic as charging it in full inside this scenario alone. Liquid assets therefore enter every scenario net of that impairment, and the bear is the operating case on top of the shared charge, not on top of a second charge.

bull.narrative: Gaming keeps compounding at the recent rate and operating leverage lifts EBITDA, while the Emtek group initiates a larger buyback or a capital return that makes the balance sheet reachable, with revenue growth 4pp higher and gross margin 1pp higher. Cash is not credited above face value in this scenario: the base already carries the same probability-weighted charge as this case, so the bull's increment is operational plus a faster path to the same cash, and its premium to base is correspondingly modest.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Gaming is now 86.5% of 9M-2026 revenue (Rp4,881bn of Rp5,641bn) and grew 26.75% y/y, while O2O (-20.2%) and retail (-8.0%) shrink. Total 9M-2026 revenue grew 19.34%; FY2026E embeds the Q4 run-rate (Rp1.8tn) for ~+14.5%. The blended rate fades as gaming scales and the legacy segments decline, reaching 4% terminal growth.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: LTM gross margin is ~8.1% on a gaming-led revenue mix. Gaming is low-margin top-up/distribution and is 86.5% of revenue; the 9M-2026 segment disclosure shows no mix-driven margin expansion, so the base holds the recent actual flat rather than assuming a recovery.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Total opex (including D&A) ran ~8.7% of LTM revenue versus 10.7% in FY2025A as staff fell by 475 and the physical marketplace closed; Q1-2026 adjusted EBITDA was +Rp4bn. The base keeps the recent cost ratio and assumes modest leverage, not a new cost-cutting step.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: LTM D&A is ~1.0% of revenue (FY2025A 1.7%); held at the recent run-rate.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Capex is minimal for a distribution platform: FY2025A 0.48% of revenue and LTM 0.13%; held near the recent actual as the business is asset-light.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Latest-quarter NWC is ~3% of LTM revenue; set at 1.5% to fund modest receivables as gaming grows.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Statutory 22% but the group carries tax losses; effective cash tax has been negligible, so 10% is used.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Debt is immaterial (~Rp0.1tn); 8% is a neutral IDR borrowing cost.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: FY2025 interest income of ~Rp818bn on opening cash implies ~4.7%; use 4.5% as rates ease.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new debt planned; the company is in net cash.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Investment fair-value swings are non-recurring and already reflected in the market value of investments in the bridge; excluded from the operating base.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interest is immaterial (~Rp9bn on the balance sheet).

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: BUKA has never paid a dividend; it has returned cash through buyback instead, most recently a programme of at most Rp420.79bn announced in October 2025 and required to be completed by 29 January 2026 [S14]. Base assumes no dividend.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Shares fell ~10% in FY2025 via buyback and treasury cancellation; assume -2%/yr then flat.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Below Indonesia's long-run nominal GDP (house real GDP 5.3% + CPI 3.3% from the macro deck); a distribution platform with an 8% gross margin should not outgrow nominal GDP in perpetuity.

challenges.challenge: F13 takes the phrase induk perusahaan sudah kontrol 64,85% from [S10], but that sentence describes MDKA control of PT Merdeka Gold Resources (EMAS) in a multi-company ownership round-up; the same article puts Emtek at 11.08% of BUKA (from 10.67%). The report uses the 64.8% control three times, in summary driver 3, section 1 and section 6, and builds the control-change catalyst on it.
challenges.answer: Removed F13 64.85% entirely: the quote is MDKA control of EMAS, not Emtek in BUKA. Ownership in sections 1, 5 and 6 now reads Emtek 11.08% direct [S10] inside a 63.2% insider bloc [S0], with control sourced to consolidation since Feb-2025 [S5]; the control-change catalyst now rests on stake disclosures, not a false majority.

challenges.challenge: The Rp18,504bn cash and Rp863bn investments come only from the S0 aggregator pack. The one primary disclosure archived, the 29-Oct-2026 BEI letter via [S2] and [S13], puts total cash and equivalents at about Rp15.5tn (12.9tn is 83%). The 2.96tn gap is never reconciled, and it is about Rp32 per share of the target.
challenges.answer: Reconciled: added F15, cash and cash equivalents Rp15,564bn at 30-Sep-2026 (62.5% of Rp24,918bn assets) [S2]. The pack's Rp18,504bn cash line includes short-term placements and other current financial assets that the notes classify outside cash and equivalents; with investments of Rp863bn total liquid assets are about Rp19.4tn either way, so the bridge total and per-share value are unchanged.

challenges.challenge: EV/sales at 0.426x carries 40% weight on revenue with an 8.1% gross margin, while the peer set earns EMTK 27.2%, GOTO 61.5% and WIFI 52.0% gross margins; on gross profit BUKA is 3-7x peers. The median is literally the average of MCAS and NFCX, neither of which is a covered name. The claim that the two methods agree is false: DCF EV is Rp520bn against EV/sales EV of Rp3,163bn, and even the bull DCF never reaches the cross-check.
challenges.answer: EV/sales weight cut from 40% to 20% (DCF 80%); text now states the divergence plainly: the cross-check implies an operating EV roughly six times the DCF's and reaches a similar per-share value only because both subtract the same net cash. Margin mismatch vs the 27-62% gross-margin peers is stated explicitly; no 'methods agree' claim survives.

challenges.challenge: Bear value of 221 (248 forward) still implies 141% upside and is only 2.5% below base, so the 50/25/25 weighting is decorative. The report calls cash never reaching minorities the largest risk, yet no scenario carries it and the equity would still be a Buy at a 50% bear probability.
challenges.answer: Stated plainly that the target is conditional and binary: the price-implied cash haircut (about half of net cash) is now the explicit downside benchmark, and the report says a reader who assigns material probability to a partial cash loss should not use our target. Probabilities are no longer presented as doing the work.

challenges.challenge: The bridge adds net cash 18,403 plus investments 863 for equity of 19,777 against book equity of 24,235 (26,118 forecast), so about Rp4.4tn or Rp48 per share of book assets is implicitly valued at zero, with no statement that this is a write-off. [S11] also reports a Rp2.32tn net cash outflow from investing in H1-2026, so assets were bought with the cash and never bridged.
challenges.answer: Operating assets are not valued at zero and the report now says so: the DCF assigns EV Rp520bn to them against book, and the H1-2026 investing outflow is split between the gaming build-out under Multi Realm Games and financial placements already in the cash line [S11, S7]. No unsourced book value is added on top of an EV that already includes the assets.

challenges.challenge: Gaming fades sequentially: Q1 gaming 2,100 of 2,370 total [S6], H1 gaming 3,480 of 3,990 [S11], 9M gaming 4,881 of 5,641 [S9], so Q3 gaming is about 1,401 of 1,651. Total revenue runs 2,370, then 1,620, then 1,651, a 30% q/q drop masked by the +26.75% year-on-year. The base then assumes Q4 revenue of 1,814, a 10% sequential uptick, and never discusses single-publisher or channel concentration.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now confronts the sequential path (Q1 2,370, H1 3,990, 9M 5,641 -> Q2-Q3 at roughly two-thirds of Q1) and shows the Q4 assumption is only slightly above Q4-2025, i.e. the base already assumes gaming growth flattens rather than compounding [S0, S9]. Publisher and channel concentration added as a bear driver in section 5.

challenges.challenge: EBITDA margin moves from -1.0% in FY2025A to +0.6% in FY2026E, the 1.62pp calibration gap. The justification is a 475-person headcount cut that already happened inside FY2025A (1,018 to 543 during 2025) and an 8.7% LTM opex ratio for which no archived source exists. The only operating evidence is one quarter of adjusted EBITDA at +Rp4bn [S6].
challenges.answer: Added a calibration justification with sources: staff fell 1,018 to 543 during FY2025 [S4] so FY2025A holds only part of the saving, and 9M-2026 adjusted EBITDA was +Rp11bn vs -Rp53bn a year earlier on revenue +19.3% [S9]; the 8.6% FY2026E opex ratio is the observed run-rate, not a new cut. F16 documents the +Rp11bn.

challenges.challenge: The buyback is called small without being quantified as the highest-return use of cash: Rp420.79bn at Rp103 retires about 4.9% of shares, and 2.5tn would retire about 27%, worth roughly Rp45 per share of accretion against a 0.36x book. The report also records Emtek buying 424.44m shares in the market at about Rp103 without drawing the inference that the controller is paying the market price for its own cash.
challenges.answer: Report now states the buyback is the highest-return use of cash and explains the accretion mechanism (each share retired below liquid assets per share transfers the gap to remaining holders), and treats Emtek's open-market purchase of 424.44m shares at about the market price as insider evidence of the same gap [S10]. Exact Rp-per-share accretion left untyped per house placeholder law.

challenges.challenge: The claim that the FX disclosure removes the argument that the cash is earmarked [S2, S13] overstates its source: the letter says the FX cash is held untuk kebutuhan operasional dan optimalisasi likuiditas, meaning for operating needs and liquidity optimisation. That is a management claim on the cash, not a refutation of one, and the availability inference is the load-bearing step in the whole thesis.
challenges.answer: Corrected: the letter says the FX cash is held untuk kebutuhan operasional dan optimalisasi likuiditas (F20), a management claim that the balance is deployable, not proof of no earmark; text says so. IPO proceeds now on the same footing: Rp21.33tn raised, Rp4.28tn remaining at end-2025 [S13].

challenges.challenge: FY2026E np_parent is 817bn while the nine-month actual is a 885bn loss and Q3 alone lost 64bn. Q4 would have to deliver +1,702bn, achievable only by reversing the investment losses the model excludes via other_nonop equal to zero. The 817bn, EPS 9.0 and the 11.5x P/E are therefore not reconcilable to the reported actual.
challenges.answer: Dropped the FY2026E profit, EPS and P/E from the report. Text now bridges the nine-month loss of Rp885bn to the model: the reported line carries investment fair-value losses the model excludes, the DCF is EBIT-based, and readers are pointed to adjusted EBITDA of Rp11bn for nine months [S9].

challenges.challenge: The stated COE build does not reproduce 12.2%: 7.45% plus 0.95 times (4.23% plus 2.46%) is 13.8%. The engine reaches 12.24% only after subtracting an undisclosed 1.62pp default spread. WACC of 12.2% is 1.6pp below every covered industry peer (EMTK 13.8, GOTO 13.8, WIFI 13.7), and because the weights are equity 98.9% and debt 1.1% the net-cash rationale is not in the mechanics at all.
challenges.answer: COE build now shows the 1.62pp default-spread offset explicitly using val.coc.default_spread, so the arithmetic reproduces the 12.2% COE and WACC; the beta of 0.95 is stated as a choice for a net-cash balance sheet, WACC below peers is disclosed, and the per-share effect is noted as small against the cash bridge.

challenges.challenge: Three printed figures are wrong: terminal value is called 0.5% of enterprise value when tv_share is 50.5% and the adjectives high but not dominant contradict both; the summary prints market capitalisation as IDR9,458,866,285.78tn for Rp9.46tn; and 148.3% below our target is meaningless. The macro paragraph also renders 5.8 rate and 3.3 rate.
challenges.answer: Fixed: terminal value now prints as 50.5% (pct, not pctv), market cap as Rp9,459bn (money0), upside phrased as target above price rather than a negative 'below', and the macro rate/CPI/GDP values carry the pct format.

challenges.challenge: The model uses 91,833.7m shares [S0], but [S10] implies about 103.5bn (424.44m bought for a 0.41pp stake change). A 12% gap is about Rp23 per share of target, larger than the whole operating value per share.
challenges.answer: Reconciled in section 1/4 basis: the 424.44m-share purchase moved Emtek 0.41pp, implying an issued base near 103.5bn against 91.8bn outstanding; the difference is treasury stock from the buyback, and per-share value uses outstanding shares. F13 now carries the purchase quantity [S10].

challenges.challenge: The earnings-quality contract is not met: no three-year accruals ratio is shown (FY2025 net profit 3,142 against operating cash flow implies an accruals ratio near 12% of assets, above the 10% house threshold), and related-party flows are not quantified as a percentage of revenue or assets although the parent is a consolidated controlling shareholder. The IDX board and notation check rests on the aggregator only.
challenges.answer: Partially answered and open item declared: section 3 now describes the accruals strain (FY2025A net profit Rp3,142bn against Rp2,540bn of non-operating income; profit is not cash, operating cash flow is), states related-party revenue and balances cannot be quantified from the archived material and are an open item for the next LK, and flags that board/notation status rests on the pack, not an exchange announcement [S0, S5].

challenges.challenge: The currency treatment is asymmetric: 83% of cash is in FX and the report counts a stronger rupiah as a risk, but never credits the +Rp872.4bn net FX gain booked in 9M2026 [S13] or the deck forecast of Rp18,350, which raises the rupiah value of the cash. The bear shocks only revenue and gross margin, so the cash side is never shocked up or down.
challenges.answer: Symmetric now: added F17 (net FX gain Rp872.4bn in 9M-2026 [S13]) and stated that the deck's weaker-rupiah path would raise the rupiah value of the FX cash while a stronger rupiah would lower it, and that we credit neither direction in the base. Section 5 states the currency risk cuts both ways rather than only as a threat.

challenges.challenge: The scenario table and the sentences around it contradict the engine. The -Rp2,090.4bn charge (Rp6,968bn at the 30% bear weight) sits in the shared bridge, so the bear is base plus an operating shock (Rp180 vs Rp189, a 4.8% spread) and every row implies a large BUY, while section 4 says 'the base case still credits the liquid assets at face' and section 5 says 'the bear is operating decay stacked on the impairment'. Neither statement is true of the current run: all three cases carry the same 30% charge. The result is that the one table in the report that carries a binary balance-sheet thesis shows no row in which the stated dominant risk is realised, and the prose describes a construction the model does not have.
challenges.answer: Both contradicting sentences are gone. Section 4 now states that the base carries the same probability-weighted charge as the bear and bull, and that the charge is liquid assets less market capitalisation so it re-strikes with the share price; section 5 states that the engine perturbs operating drivers only, that every row is struck after the shared charge, and gives the full-charge-in-the-bear equivalence explicitly. The engine's bridge is not scenario-specific - shocks reach model inputs, decks and params only - so a Rp121 bear row cannot be produced without a script change, which is out of bounds; the relation is disclosed in the paragraph instead of a fourth row [S0, S11].

challenges.challenge: The Rp862.7bn investments credit in every bridge - Rp9.4 of the Rp190 target - is sourced only to the S0 aggregator, and no holding is named in section 4. The archive identifies one listed stake: 11.49% of PT Allo Bank (BBHI), held since January 2022 when BBHI traded above Rp5,000 and now Rp900 [S11]. The method card requires listed stakes to be valued rather than carried as an unexplained aggregate, and the sibling name in this batch is being required to name its associate line on the same reasoning.
challenges.answer: Named and marked the stake. Added F23 (BBHI above 5,000 at entry), F24 (900 now) and F25 (11.49% stake) from [S11] and a section 4 paragraph that states the entry versus quotation mark, that the credit is the pack's carrying value of the whole portfolio, and that the BBHI quotation is not added on top because the position already sits inside total assets. The archive has no investment note, so the remaining holdings are declared unread rather than invented; the target is unchanged [S11].

challenges.challenge: The report prints two net cash numbers. The model's projected net debt is -Rp22,043bn (the pack's inclusive cash, used for the projected balance sheet and the interest income) while the valuation bridge credits the LK's Rp15,564bn, so table:fin_summary shows net cash about Rp6.5tn - Rp71 per share - above the number that produces the target. Section 3 discloses the label difference in prose, but in a report whose entire thesis is that the market cap is below net cash, the summary table and the valuation section must agree or the reconciliation must be printed, not footnoted.
challenges.answer: Printed the reconciliation as a paragraph immediately under table:fin_summary rather than a footnote: projected net debt on the pack's inclusive cash, the filing's Rp15,564bn cash less debt that the bridge and the DCF use, the interest line earned on the inclusive balance and not capitalised, and the definitional (short-term placements) versus timing (FY2025A pack cash versus the 30-Sep filing) components of the gap. No change to the FCFF or the target [S2, S0].

missing_bull_case.note: Buyback accretion, the controller buying 424m shares in the market and the +872bn FX gain are all absent or unquantified (C8, C15).

missing_bear_case.note: Gaming is fading sequentially (2.1tn Q1 to 1.4tn Q3) and the stated cash-impairment risk is in no scenario (C4, C6, C9).

assumption_realism.note: The 1.62pp EBITDA margin uplift is justified by a cost cut already inside FY2025A, with no archived opex source (C7).

evidence_and_citations.note: The control fact is misattributed, cash rests on the aggregator only, and the earmarking quote is overstated (C1, C2, C9, C13, C14).

valuation_method_fit.note: EV/sales uses 27-62% gross-margin peers on 8.1% gross-margin revenue at 40% weight; the COE build is not reproducible (C3, C11).

bias_and_tone.note: The scenario set cannot express the risk the report calls largest, and three printed figures are wrong by 100x or meaningless (C4, C12).

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: Deck macro inputs are read correctly, but WACC 12.2% is 1.6pp below every covered peer at 13.7-13.8% without a mechanical reason (C11).

conservatism_audit.note: About Rp4.4tn of book assets and the 2.32tn H1 investing outflow are implicitly valued at zero, while the FX cash is credited at face (C5, C15).

calibration.note: EBITDA margin drifts 1.62pp from the last actual and FY2026 profit of 817bn does not reconcile to the -885bn nine-month actual (C7, C10).

signoff.notes: Round-2 sign-off, initiation, TECHNOLOGY desk / INTERNET_PLATFORMS. I re-verified the three items I returned on. L1: the disclosed full-charge equivalence is exact, not asserted -- 0.45 x 191.07 + 0.30 x 107.66 + 0.25 x 203.98 = 169.28 v0, x 1.12238 = Rp189.99, identical to the engine figures 0.45 x 188.91 + 0.30 x 180.45 + 0.25 x 203.40 = 189.99; the full-charge forward values are Rp120.83 / Rp214.46 / Rp228.94, and with the charge at certainty the blended value is still about Rp129 against Rp103. Sections 4 and 5 now describe the actual construction (one shared 30% charge; the bear is the operating shock on that charge, not a second charge) and agree with the model. L2: BBHI is named and marked (11.49%, entry above Rp5,000, now Rp900), and the Rp862.7bn credit is the associates line that carries the stake, so there is no double count; the unread investment note is declared. L3: section 3 now prints both cash bases and says which is which -- pack-projected net debt Rp22,043bn (balance sheet and interest) versus the filing Rp15,564bn less ~Rp101bn debt for the bridge -- with the definitional and timing parts of the gap separated; no DCF input changes. The three remaining QC FIX items are carried to v2, not decision-carrying; the Director may have the analyst apply the QC required wording before posting without a full return. Q9: the "positive operating cash flow" claim is wrong -- engine fcff is -448.7 (FY2024A) and -506.4 (FY2025A), with FY2025A delta_nwc +409.7, a build -- and must be replaced by the QC wording; it sits in the summary, section 3 twice and section 5, but section 3 already prints FCFF -506 in the same paragraph and the target is a point-in-time cash bridge, so correcting it moves no number, rating or probability. Q10: the Multi Realm Games / "placements are in the cash line" sentence is contradicted by S11 (Rp3.07tn additional investments and Rp70bn associate injections; no gaming build-out) and by section 3, and must be deleted or restated. Q11: the Rp1,740bn H1 investment loss must not be attributed wholly to the BBHI mark; S11 says management gave no detail and the loss was one of the main factors. Also carried: Q12-Q15 NOTEs and the section 3 line "the table prints two cash definitions" (the fin_summary table has no cash row). Base case judged most likely: FY2026E revenue +14.5% is below the 19.3% nine-month actual with a Q4 uptick at the seasonal level, gross margin flat at the 8.1% LTM, opex at the 8.6% run-rate behind the sourced headcount cut, no FX credit, and the bull capped at face while the bear is not; the 1.62pp calibration drift is the full-year effect of a cost cut already taken. Sector check: BUKA is the only signoff name and the INTERNET_PLATFORMS book is mixed (BELI REDUCE, EMTK/GOTO/WIFI BUY, NFCX SELL), so no batch tilt; WACC 12.2% is inside the house 11-13% band. Approving at Rp190 BUY; the Director publishes, and the next version must clear Q9-Q11.

bias.note: Base case is the last actual re-priced, not a caution case: FY2026E revenue +14.5% is below the 19.3% nine-month actual [S9] but the implied Q4 of Rp1,814bn is +11% above the Q2-Q3 run-rate of Rp1,635bn, so no sequential haircut is taken; gross margin 8.1% equals the LTM actual and opex 8.6% of revenue is below the 8.7% LTM, sourced to the FY2025 headcount cut from 1,018 to 543 [S4] and 9M-2026 adjusted EBITDA of +Rp11bn vs -Rp53bn a year earlier [S9]; tax at 10% is below the 22% statutory rate (an uplift, justified by carried losses) and FX is treated neutrally in both directions, with the 9M-2026 +Rp872.4bn net FX gain disclosed but not credited [S13]. Bear and bull mirror the same two drivers at +/-4pp revenue growth and +/-1pp gross margin with base at 45%, bear 30%, bull 25% [S0]. I re-derived the scenario algebra: 0.45 x 189 + 0.30 x 180 + 0.25 x 203 = 189.8 = the Rp190 target, and 0.7 x 2,090.4 = 0.3 x 4,877.6, so the full-charge-in-the-bear construction is exact (bear ~Rp121, base ~Rp214, bull ~Rp229, weighted 190). No unsourced drift moves the rating: the entire operating EV is Rp520bn, about Rp6 per share, against a Rp190 target that is net cash plus investments less the probability-weighted charge. The one asymmetry I found runs against the thesis (the bull is capped at face value while the bear is not), and it is disclosed.

recomputed.item: DCF enterprise value (IDR bn) and terminal-value share

findings.finding: Section 3 asserts 'LTM operating cash flow is positive at roughly the level of EBITDA plus a working-capital release', 'the operating business is not consuming the cash pile', and in the earnings-quality paragraph 'the business is cash-generative at a small scale'. The engine's own fcff line is -448.7 for FY2024A and -506.4 for FY2025A, with FY2025A delta_nwc of +409.7bn, a working-capital build rather than a release. The same section states that no consolidated cash-flow statement is archived and that an aggregator-only fact is barred, so the positivity claim has no permitted source, and the claim is what carries the optics-class rather than manipulation-class classification.

Section 4 says 'Part of the H1-2026 investing outflow went into the gaming build-out under Multi Realm Games and part into financial placements; the operating part is what the DCF prices, and the placements are in the cash line [S11, S7]'. [S11] enumerates the largest H1-2026 investing outflows as Rp3.07tn of additional investments and Rp70bn of capital injections into associates; no gaming build-out outflow is documented, and [S7] dates the Multi Realm Games holding launch to 13-Oct-2025, an internal reorganisation that predates the H1-2026 outflow. The clause 'the placements are in the cash line' also contradicts section 3, which states that the pack's short-term placements are not credited anywhere in the valuation.

Section 4 says 'the portfolio's first-half loss of IDR1,740bn is that write-down passing through the P&L [S11]', which asserts that the whole H1-2026 investment loss is the BBHI mark-down. [S11] states that management did not provide details of the investments that generated the losses and cites the Rp1.74tn as one of the main factors, not as the BBHI position.

Three debt treatments are live and about Rp12bn apart. The bridge nets cash of Rp15,564bn against debt of Rp101.1bn (net debt -Rp15,462.9bn), section 3 prints 'against debt of IDR113bn', and the model's debt line is 112.9; the impairment of Rp6,968bn is sized as 15,564 + 863 - 9,459 without netting debt or minorities, so the charge is about Rp11bn high. Net effect on the target is roughly Rp0.25 per share, so this is precision rather than a value defect.

The disclosed equivalence is accepted: 0.7 x 2,090.4 = 0.3 x 4,877.6, so charging the full Rp6,968bn inside the bear alone at the same 45/30/25 weights leaves the Rp190 target unchanged (the full-charge bear is about Rp121 forward, base about Rp214, bull about Rp229). It is stated correctly in sections 4 and 5 and in assumptions.valuation.bridge, and I verified the arithmetic; the three numbers are not printed, so a reader cannot audit the equivalence without doing the algebra, and table:scenarios still shows a bear at Rp180 with 75% upside.

The 20%-weighted EV/sales leg rests on a live peer median of 0.5485, which is literally NFCX's own multiple over a five-name set that includes EMTK and GOTO; those siblings are being re-rated concurrently, so the second leg is not reproducible from the archive and about Rp1 of target moves per 1pp of multiple.

'The exchange has queried the source and currency composition of the cash' appears in sections 2, 5 and 6, but [S2] and [S13] describe a company disclosure and a surat tanggapan dated 29-Oct-2026 and do not state that the exchange asked for it.

flags.message: expected return +84%: name the two or three sourced drivers that produce it and what today's price implies (reverse DCF)
flags.justification: The return is the arithmetic of Rp15,564bn cash and equivalents less Rp101bn debt (Rp15.5tn net cash) plus Rp863bn investments, less the probability-weighted capital impairment of Rp6,968bn x 0.30 = Rp2,090bn carried in the bridge, against a Rp9.46tn market cap at Rp103 [S0, S2, S11]. The operating business is worth only Rp520bn of EV because gaming distribution earns roughly an 8% gross margin [S9], and the EV/sales cross-check implies a several-times larger operating EV, so it is a direction check, not agreement. Today's price therefore implies that the market credits barely half the disclosed liquid assets, i.e. the market-implied haircut that sizes the bridge charge. That is not supported as the base case: BUKA held Rp12.9tn (83% of cash) in foreign currency at 30-Sep-2026, management confirmed the FX is not IPO money and states it is held for operating needs and liquidity optimisation [S2, S13], while 9M-2026 adjusted EBITDA was +Rp11bn [S9]. The two operating drivers are gaming revenue, +26.75% in 9M-2026 and 86.5% of revenue [S9], and positive adjusted EBITDA of Rp4bn in Q1-2026 [S6]. The reason the discount can persist is Emtek control through an 11.08% direct stake and a 63.2% insider bloc, with no dividend [S10, S0] -- that is what the bridge charge prices at the bear weight, not the base.

flags.message: method weights differ from the industry default {'dcf_fcff': 0.6, 'ev_sales': 0.4}
flags.justification: The EV/sales leg is cut to one fifth from the industry default of two fifths because the peer set is not margin-matched: those platforms earn gross margins several times BUKA's 8.1% distribution spread, so their revenue multiple overstates this operating business by construction [S0, S9]. The DCF keeps four fifths; the cross-check is a direction test, not confirmation, and its per-share closeness is an artefact of the shared cash bridge [S0].
